items.abstract: <jats:p>A variety of experimental studies has suggested that Down's syndrome children perform at an inferior level relative to expected performance for their Mental Age. Comparative studies addressing this question have typically employed MA‐matching procedures of questionable validity and have utilized experimental measures of unknown ecological validity. In the present study 24 pairs of Down's syndrome preschool and non‐handicapped children were matched to MA as assessed by the Mental Scale of the Bayley Scale of Infant Development. An item‐by‐item analysis of the relative pattern of passes and fails on the scale indicated that despite the overall MA‐match, the way in which the global score was achieved differed in the two groups. Non‐handicapped children performed significantly better on subscales representative of fine motor development than the Down's syndrome children. The latter tended to compensate by doing somewhat better on language items, though not significantly so. All children executed a series of simple manipulative tasks analogous to a typical nursery toy (placing rods in holes). The imbalance in the matching appeared to carry through to performance on this task since the non‐handicapped children tended to execute both phases of the task more quickly than their Down's syndrome peers. With regard to prehension, however, the groups did not differ with respect to sophistication of grip, though in one case the Down's children employed a more advanced palmar grip. Hand measurements were taken to see if this difference could be accounted for by greater maturation in the Down's syndrome group. This was found not to be the case, and the possible influence of greater experience of the relatively older Down's syndrome children is considered. Multiple influences on fine motor skill and its development are discussed, and alternatives to MA‐matching considered.</jats:p>
title: Prehensile development in Down's syndrome and non‐handicapped preschool children

items.abstract: <jats:p>The effects of short range solvent structure and short range dynamical correlations are investigated for the steady state rate constant k for solution reactions influenced by diffusion. The description is in terms of a Smoluchowski equation describing relative motion of two molecules in an outer spatial translational region, supplemented by a sink term that accounts for dynamics in an inner reaction zone. In the outer region, solvent structural effects are included by a potential of mean force, which exhibits a short range well and barrier combination leading to ’’potential caging.’’ Outer region short range dynamical correlations are included via a separation-dependent diffusion coefficient, leading to ’’dynamical caging’’ as relative motion is showed at small separations. These two short range effects are neglected in standard diffusion treatments. We find that k is only modestly influenced by the above short range effects. In order to expose short range structure and correlation influence in a more sensitive way, we formulate the short range caging picture. This information focuses on events occuring at the small separations usually implied by the term ’’solvent cage.’’ At this level of description, short range effects are clearly revealed. We compare our formulation with the encounter formulation of Noyes.</jats:p>
title: Short range caging effects for reactions in solution. I. Reaction rate constants and short range caging picture

items.abstract: <jats:p>The prehensile grasp of 24 normal and 45 cerebral palsied young children was studied by the use of cinema-analysis technique. A group of 18 diplegics of the cerebral palsy group were analyzed and yielded a description of the most prevalent abnormalities of function. Some physiological and developmental relationships are discussed. A case is presented which illustrates the clinical implications of recognition of the subtle manifestions of neurological abnormalities.</jats:p>
title: THE PREHENSILE GRASP OF SPASTIC DIPLEGIA
